original: Modern multi-device environments, encompassing smartphones, personal computers and embedded endpoints, frequently demand tight local network interoperability for telemetry, continuous synchronization and remote peripheral control. However, establishing mutual trust among heterogeneous devices on a local area network (LAN) exposes a usable-security trilemma: system designers are forced to trade off decentralization (zero cloud dependency), cryptographic integrity (man-in-the-middle resistance and certificate pinning) and frictionless usability (constant human pairing effort per device). Existing solutions either rely on centralized identity providers that compromise user privacy and introduce wide-area failure modes, or enforce pairwise trust-on-first-use (TOFU), whose human pairing effort grows quadratically with the number of devices. This paper proposes Transitive Trust-on-First-Use (T-TOFU), a zero-coordinator trust propagation and state synchronization protocol tailored for personal device meshes. Under T-TOFU, a single human-gated authentication ceremony transitively enrolls an incoming node across the entire mesh. A deterministic canonical pool digest, coupled with anti-entropy heartbeat gossip, maintains pool-wide consistency without an online certificate authority or central ledger, and a cascaded revocation flood purges removed endpoints. T-TOFU is implemented in Link, a cross-platform mesh runtime for Windows and Android, and is evaluated for cryptographic robustness, protocol overhead and convergence. The results show that T-TOFU reduces the total human pairing effort from quadratic to linear in the mesh size, with a single ceremony per new device, while converging across a local mesh in well under one second with negligible bandwidth overhead.
revised: Personal device meshes need local communication for telemetry, synchronization and remote peripheral control. Establishing trust across these devices requires balancing cloud independence, cryptographic authentication and the effort of manual pairing. Pairwise trust-on-first-use (TOFU) requires a separate ceremony for every pair in a fully connected mesh, so the total pairing effort grows quadratically with mesh size. We present Transitive Trust-on-First-Use (T-TOFU), a protocol that enrolls a new device through one human-gated pairing ceremony with an existing member. Trusted members then exchange certificate records over authenticated TLS connections. A canonical pool digest and anti-entropy heartbeat gossip detect and repair differences between trust tables without an online certificate authority or central ledger; a revocation flood removes a device from the reachable mesh. We implement T-TOFU in Link for Windows and Android and analyze its security under the stated adversary model. Building an $N$-device mesh requires $N-1$ human pairing ceremonies, with one ceremony for each additional device. In the four-node physical testbed, mean enrollment convergence was $48.2\,\text{ms}$ and revocation propagated in under $65\,\text{ms}$. A 98-byte heartbeat sent every 2 seconds accounts for about $0.05\,\text{KB/s}$ per connection.
reason: Replace the generic opening and qualitative performance language with the protocol operations, ceremony count, and measurements already reported in Section V. State the fully connected baseline and distinguish security analysis from measurement.

location: I-A. Limitations of Current Paradigms, paragraph 2

original: Conversely, open-source peer-to-peer (P2P) systems (e.g., KDE Connect \cite{kdeconnect}, SSH-based local tooling, standard Bluetooth pairing \cite{antonioli2023bluffs}) adopt a Trust-on-First-Use (TOFU) model using self-signed cryptographic certificates or pre-shared keys. While these systems achieve zero-cloud privacy, they suffer from an $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ human pairing bottleneck: enrolling $N$ devices requires $\binom{N}{2} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2}$ independent, manual PIN verification or QR code scanning ceremonies. For an ordinary user with five personal devices, completing ten discrete manual pairing operations introduces severe friction, and in practice users rarely perform the fingerprint verification that TOFU relies on \cite{neef2022ssh}.
revised: Pairwise approaches establish trust separately between devices. Examples include KDE Connect \cite{kdeconnect}, SSH-based local tooling and Bluetooth pairing \cite{antonioli2023bluffs}, although their authentication mechanisms differ. In a fully connected mesh using manual pairwise TOFU, enrolling $N$ devices requires $\binom{N}{2} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2}$ pairing ceremonies. Five devices therefore require ten ceremonies. Manual fingerprint checking also depends on user attention; SSH users may accept an unfamiliar host key without verifying it \cite{neef2022ssh}.
reason: Make the fully connected assumption explicit, retain the exact count, and avoid classifying every Bluetooth method as TOFU. Replace the unmeasured severity claim and universal user-behavior claim with the SSH-specific issue discussed by the cited paper.

If a remote device presents a certificate whose fingerprint differs from the stored pinned value, the connection is instantly aborted with an alert.

original: This paper presented \textbf{Transitive Trust-on-First-Use (T-TOFU)}, a decentralized trust federation protocol that resolves the classical Usable-Security Trilemma in personal device meshes. By combining human-gated root pairing, canonical pool digest gossip and cascaded revocation, T-TOFU eliminates the $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ pairing barrier while preserving zero-cloud decentralization and strict cryptographic integrity. We verified T-TOFU through a reference implementation across Windows and Android, demonstrating sub-second convergence and resilience against local network adversaries.
revised: T-TOFU establishes trust in a personal device mesh through human-verified pairing with one existing member, followed by certificate propagation over authenticated TLS connections. Canonical pool digests support anti-entropy repair, and cascaded revocation removes a device from the reachable mesh. This design requires $N-1$ human ceremonies to build an $N$-device mesh, compared with $N(N-1)/2$ for fully connected pairwise TOFU, while keeping trust management local. In the four-node Windows and Android testbed, mean enrollment convergence was $48.2\,\text{ms}$ and revocation propagated in under $65\,\text{ms}$. These measurements characterize the evaluated testbed; the security analysis addresses local network adversaries under the stated assumptions.
reason: Summarize the mechanism, exact ceremony counts and reported observations. Replace sweeping resolution and verified-resilience language with the scope of the implementation, testbed and security analysis. Future work remains unchanged.
